slides.text: Every value in Go has a type, and Go checks it before the program runs. Here you use whole numbers, decimals, text and bools, convert between them by hand, and read the errors Go reports when types do not fit. The snippet is a map of the types, not Go.
slides.code:
whole numbers  int, int8, int64, uint8
decimals       float64
text           string
true or false  bool

exercises.title: Whole numbers
exercises.guide: Declare two whole numbers of different types and print them.

chunks.guide: `int` is the usual type for whole numbers.
Other types have a fixed size and range. `uint8` holds 0 to 255: the `u` means unsigned, so no negatives.

notes.text: A small number that is never negative.

chunks.guide: Print both.

exercises.title: Fit the number
exercises.guide: Pick a type that can hold 200.

exercises.title: Decimal numbers
exercises.guide: Declare two decimal numbers and print them.

chunks.guide: A number with a decimal point is a `float64`, the usual type for decimals.

notes.text: A number with a dot becomes a float64.

chunks.guide: A whole number also fits a `float64`: it is a decimal with nothing after the point.

notes.text: A whole number can fill a float64.

chunks.guide: A decimal that is whole prints without the point.

exercises.title: Why does it not compile?
exercises.guide: Read the message, then pick the cause.
exercises.code:
./main.go:8:14: invalid operation:
  count + price (mismatched types
  int and float64)
options: An int and a float64 cannot be added directly
exercises.explanation: Go never mixes number types on its own. Convert one side so both have the same type.

exercises.title: Convert a number
exercises.guide: Turn an `int` into a `float64`, and a `float64` into an `int`.

chunks.guide: A type used like a function converts the value. `count` itself stays an `int`.

notes.text: Makes a decimal copy of the value.

chunks.guide: A decimal to convert.
Going back to `int` cuts off the decimals. It does not round.

notes.text: Cuts off the decimals, with no rounding.

chunks.guide: Print both results.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `uint8` holds 0 to 255. `big` is a variable, so Go does not stop it: 300 wraps around to 300 - 256 = 44.

exercises.title: Text and bools
exercises.guide: Declare a string and a bool, and ask the string for its length.

chunks.guide: Text is a `string`, written between double quotes.
`len` gives the length of a string, counted in bytes. Each of these letters is one byte.

notes.text: Built into Go, so it needs no import.

chunks.guide: A `bool` is `true` or `false`, and nothing else.

notes.text: A bool value; the other one is true.

chunks.guide: Print the three values.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `len` counts bytes, not letters. The letter `é` takes two bytes, so the five letters make 6 bytes.

exercises.title: A single character
exercises.guide: Store one character and print it in two ways.

chunks.guide: Single quotes make a **rune**: one character, kept as its Unicode number.
A rune prints as its number. `G` is 71.
Converting the rune to a `string` gives the character back as text.

notes.text: Turns the character into a one-letter string.

exercises.title: A true or false value
exercises.guide: Go never turns a number into a bool. Give `open` a bool value.

slides.text: Whole numbers come in fixed sizes. A bigger size holds more but takes more space, and a value that does not fit wraps around instead of failing. Unsigned types start at 0 and reach twice as high. The snippet is a map of the ranges, not Go.
slides.code:
int8    -128 to 127
uint8   0 to 255
int16   -32768 to 32767
int32   about -2 to 2 billion
int64   about -9 to 9 quintillion

exercises.title: Sized integers
exercises.guide: Declare whole numbers of every size.

chunks.guide: `int8` takes 8 bits and holds -128 to 127. That is its whole range.

notes.text: Takes 8 bits, so it holds -128 to 127.

chunks.guide: `int16` holds up to 32767.

notes.text: Takes 16 bits, so it holds up to 32767.

chunks.guide: `int32` reaches about 2 billion. `int64` reaches about 9 quintillion, so 5 billion fits.

notes.text: Takes 32 bits, up to about 2 billion.
Takes 64 bits, the largest signed size.

chunks.text:
var large int32 = 100000
    var huge int64 = 5000000000

chunks.guide: `uint` is the unsigned twin of `int`: never negative. `int` and `uint` have the size of the machine, 64 bits on most.
Print them all.
`byte` is used for raw data. A character like `'G'` is just the number 71, which fits.
`byte` and `uint8` are the same type, so no conversion is needed.
Both print as numbers. `rune` is the same kind of name for `int32`.

exercises.title: Match the sizes
exercises.guide: An `int` and an `int64` do not mix. Convert `a` so both sides of the sum match.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var a int = 5
    var b int64 = 7
    total := ___(a) + b
    fmt.Println(total)
}

exercises.title: Wrap around
exercises.guide: Push values past the range of an `int8`.

chunks.guide: 200 is above 127, so it wraps: 200 - 256 = -56. `big` is a variable, so Go lets it through.

notes.text: Converts to int8, so 200 wraps around.

chunks.guide: The highest value an `int8` holds.
One past the maximum wraps to the minimum. Go gives no warning.
Print both results.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: Converting to `int` cuts off the decimals, toward zero. It never rounds, not even a negative number.

exercises.title: A whole decimal constant
exercises.guide: Put whole-valued decimal constants into `int` variables.

chunks.guide: `3.0` is a constant with nothing after the point, so it fits an `int`. `2.5` would not compile: the `.5` would be lost.

notes.text: A whole-valued constant fits in an int.

chunks.guide: A named constant works the same way, since constants have no type until used.
chunks.text:
const rows = 4.0
    var count int = rows

chunks.guide: Both print as whole numbers.

exercises.title: A number as a string
exercises.guide: Convert an `int` to a `string` and see what you get.

chunks.guide: A whole number.
An `int` turned into a `string` gives the character with that number, not the digits. 72 is `H`.

notes.text: Gives a character, not the digits.

chunks.guide: The number itself is unchanged. To get the text "72" you use `strconv`, in a later course.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: An `int` converted to `string` becomes the character with that number, and 97 is `a`. For the text "97", `strconv` comes in a later course.
